title: Your Next DSL Author Is a Language Model
gist: Irakli Betchvaia argues that LLM hallucination on domain-specific languages is a training-corpus frequency problem, not a knowledge problem, and that RAG cannot fix it because retrieval grounds facts but not notation. His proposed answer, Typed Domain Grounding, embeds the domain as a typed internal DSL inside a mainstream host language so the stock compiler becomes a hallucination oracle — benchmarked on kUML at 45.3% Structural Fidelity versus 37.9% for PlantUML and 37.4% for Mermaid with Claude Sonnet 5, though the effect does not hold for every model tested.

insights.claim: LLM syntactic competence is, to a first approximation, a function of training-data frequency — models write Kotlin, TypeScript, Python and SQL reliably because those languages are dense in the corpus, and degrade into pastiche where the corpus is sparse, a relationship documented in code-LLM benchmarks that classify languages by frequency.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Reframes model capability as a data-distribution property rather than a reasoning property — predicts which developer tooling niches AI will and won't serve well without retraining.
insights.quote: Syntactic competence is, to a first approximation, a function of training-data frequency
insights.locator: Fluency Is Frequency

insights.claim: Every freshly designed external DSL has, from a model's point of view, a training-corpus frequency of zero for its exact syntax, so any new notation starts at maximum hallucination risk by construction.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Any product whose interface is a proprietary config or query language is structurally disadvantaged in an agent-authored world — a new risk factor for tooling vendors with bespoke syntaxes.
insights.quote: Every freshly designed external DSL is, from the model's point of view, a language with a training-corpus frequency of zero for its exact syntax.
insights.locator: Fluency Is Frequency

insights.claim: Transferable priors from syntactically adjacent grammars are not a rescue but the actual failure mechanism: the model smuggles in arrow syntax from Mermaid or PlantUML, invents plausible method names like addRelation or withLabel, and passes three arguments to a two-argument construct because a syntactic cousin takes three.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Explains why hallucinated DSL output looks more plausible than random errors, and therefore why human review catches it less often.
insights.quote: Each mistake is the corpus's most probable completion, applied to a language the corpus never contained. The output is fluent, well-indented, and wrong.
insights.locator: A model confronted with an unfamiliar notation does not fail loudly

insights.claim: Model failure on unfamiliar notation is silent — there is no change in tone or apparent confidence when generation degrades, which is precisely what makes the failure mode easy to miss in review.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Confidence calibration does not degrade with competence, so human-in-the-loop review is a weak control for this class of error.
insights.quote: generation degrades into pastiche, without change in tone or apparent confidence
insights.locator: Fluency Is Frequency

insights.claim: Parser leniency — a traditional DSL virtue for human authors — becomes a defect with machine authors: diagram tools and config parsers that skip unrecognized lines and render a best guess turn a hallucinated keyword into a professional-looking artifact that is quietly missing one element.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Forgiving input handling, long considered good UX, is now a correctness liability in any pipeline where models author input — a design-principle inversion with broad tooling implications.
insights.quote: For humans, that is hospitality. For machine authors, it is a trap door.
insights.locator: A traditional DSL virtue makes this problem worse: leniency

insights.claim: The human error-detection mechanism does not transfer to models: a human who mistypes notices because they intended the association, while the model intended nothing and the downstream engineer, primed by nine correct classes and clean typography, has no reason to suspect the artifact is incomplete.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Quality-control assumptions built around human authorship silently break when generation is automated — relevant to any workflow substituting models for people.
insights.quote: The model intended nothing and the engineer downstream, primed by nine correct classes and clean typography, has no reason to suspect the picture is incomplete.
insights.locator: A human who mistyped would have noticed

insights.claim: Lenient name-based diagram tools do something worse than dropping a phantom reference: many create a node the moment an edge references it, promoting a hallucinated element into a real, empty class that looks exactly as legitimate as its neighbours.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Auto-creation semantics convert model errors into durable artifacts that propagate downstream — the highest-severity version of this failure class.
insights.quote: One toolchain converts the phantom into a located error; the other converts it into furniture.
insights.locator: Phantom references die the same way

insights.claim: The author's explicit recommendation to language designers is to abolish leniency — silently fixing malformed input is a leak in the oracle, not a courtesy, so tooling should fail strictly and loudly by default.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: A concrete design mandate that runs counter to a decade of developer-experience convention; watch whether config and IaC tools start tightening validation defaults.
insights.quote: Recognize that silently "fixing" malformed input is a leak in the oracle, not a courtesy
insights.locator: Six Recommendations for Language Designers

insights.claim: RAG and Typed Domain Grounding are orthogonal and combinable: retrieval disciplines what the model says about the world (data space), while TDG anchors the notation used to express it (competence space), and a model with flawless retrieved facts can still emit a DSL statement with invented grammar.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Names a failure axis that retrieval-centric AI stacks do not address at all — a gap in the standard enterprise RAG architecture.
insights.quote: A model with flawless facts in its context can still emit a DSL statement with invented grammar.
insights.locator: Grounding the Language, Not Just the Facts

insights.claim: More prompting, longer context and better retrieval are characterized as the reflexive but non-durable fix; the durable fix is a design decision taken before the model ever sees the language — do not use a foreign syntax in the first place.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Shifts investment from runtime prompt engineering toward upstream language and API design — a different spend category with different vendors.
insights.quote: The reflexive fix is more prompting, longer context, and better retrieval. The durable fix is a design decision made before the model ever sees your language.
insights.locator: Ask a frontier language model for Python

insights.claim: Typed Domain Grounding's principle compresses to one rule: never invent syntax an LLM has never seen — embed the domain in a language it already knows and let the compiler be the oracle.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: A portable heuristic for evaluating whether any new developer-facing language or schema is fit for an agent-authored future.
insights.quote: Never invent syntax an LLM has never seen: Embed the domain in a language it already knows and let the compiler be the oracle
insights.locator: The principle fits in one sentence

insights.claim: Corpus presence is proposed as a new host-language selection criterion sitting alongside expressiveness, type-system strength and tooling — a criterion that could not have existed before LLMs, and one that gets a vote when it diverges from the classic criteria.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Language popularity now compounds: high-corpus languages get better AI support, which drives more adoption — a winner-take-more dynamic favouring Python, TypeScript and Kotlin over elegant niche languages.
insights.quote: TDG adds a criterion that couldn't have existed before LLMs: corpus presence.
insights.locator: Host Language Chosen by Training Data Affinity

insights.claim: Compiler strictness is engineered deliberately as the hallucination filter: named parameters over positional, enums over magic strings, sealed hierarchies so a hallucinated fifth variant has no type to inhabit, and receiver types so illegal nesting becomes a sentence the language cannot express.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Each API design choice decides which hallucination class becomes a compile error versus stays invisible — an actionable checklist for teams hardening APIs for agent consumption.
insights.quote: A hallucinated fifth variant has no type to inhabit.
insights.locator: The Compiler As Oracle

insights.claim: The Generate-Compile-Repair loop is not TDG's novel element — compiler-feedback repair is established self-debugging literature — but TDG puts it to double use as both a repair channel and a measurement instrument revealing how often and why a given DSL needs fixing.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Turning the repair loop into instrumentation gives teams a quantitative way to compare notations and APIs by hallucination rate — a metric nobody currently reports.
insights.locator: The Generate-Compile-Repair (GCR) Loop

insights.claim: Repair loops should be bounded and carry located diagnostics: kUML caps at three attempts, repairs that succeed tend to succeed early, and a model still failing after three rounds of located feedback is missing a concept rather than a comma.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Gives an operational stopping rule for agent retry budgets and a diagnostic for distinguishing syntax failure from comprehension failure.
insights.quote: A model still failing after three rounds of located feedback is missing a concept, not a comma.
insights.locator: The Generate-Compile-Repair (GCR) Loop

insights.claim: A callable teaching channel — implementable as a Model Context Protocol server returning a small set of curated, already-compiling examples for the construct the model needs at that moment — outperforms stuffing full API documentation into the prompt, which buries five relevant constructs under ninety-five irrelevant ones.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Concrete, measured use case for MCP beyond data access: targeted example retrieval as a context-efficiency play.
insights.locator: An On-Demand Teaching Channel

insights.claim: Embedding a DSL inside a mainstream host language inherits the entire existing toolchain on day zero — syntax highlighting, completion, jump-to-definition, safe rename, debugger and reviewer-familiar diffs — each of which would otherwise be a multi-year project for an external DSL.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: The tooling-inheritance argument, independent of AI, is already a strong build-versus-embed case — AI just adds a second, larger reason.
insights.locator: Embedded, Not External

insights.claim: In a fifty-task benchmark spanning UML, SysML v2 and C4 diagrams with Claude Sonnet 5, the compiler-checked embedded language kUML reached the highest Structural Fidelity at 45.3% versus 37.9% for PlantUML and 37.4% for Mermaid, and the lowest hallucination rate at 15.4% versus 16.5% and 21.9%.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: First quantified comparison of notation choice as an AI-reliability lever — the size of the gap (roughly 20% relative fidelity gain) sets expectations for similar redesigns.
insights.locator: The Numbers and an Honest Caveat

insights.claim: The strict approach won despite a lower first-try compile rate than the lenient tools — the strict oracle rejects more output up front and that rejection correlates with higher downstream fidelity and lower hallucination, an explicit inversion of the usual first-pass-success metric.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: First-pass success rate is a misleading KPI for agentic coding tools; optimizing for it may select for exactly the leniency that hides errors.
insights.quote: The strict oracle rejects more up front and the result correlates with higher Structural Fidelity and lower hallucination downstream.
insights.locator: The benchmark did not show a higher first-shot compile rate

insights.claim: Adding the kuml.examples teaching tool raised the SysML v2 first-compile rate after the repair loop from twenty-five percent to 87.5 percent — two of eight versus seven of eight tasks — with Claude Sonnet 5, a single run per cell, and this is a compilation result rather than a fidelity result.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: A 3.5x compile-rate jump from curated examples suggests targeted example retrieval is higher-leverage than model upgrades for niche-language tasks.
insights.quote: a kuml.examples tool raised the first-compile rate for SysML v2 diagrams from twenty-five to 87.5 percent
insights.locator: An On-Demand Teaching Channel

insights.claim: The effect is explicitly model-dependent: the full win holds for Claude Sonnet 5 and GPT-4o, but Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro and Qwen3-Coder:30b all put Mermaid or PlantUML ahead on Structural Fidelity.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Tooling architecture choices interact with model choice, so an approach validated on one model family may not transfer — a diligence trap for AI-infrastructure claims.
insights.quote: It does not hold uniformly elsewhere.
insights.locator: The public gallery now covers nine model runs

insights.claim: Grok 4 is the explicit counterexample: kUML gets its narrowest fidelity win in the study (36.8% vs 34.6% and 36.4%) while posting the study's highest hallucination rate (28.1% vs 22.4% and 23.0%) — a strict oracle without a matching payoff.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Publishing the failing case is a credibility marker; it also flags that model-specific evaluation is mandatory before committing to a DSL redesign.
insights.quote: which is a strict oracle without a matching payoff
insights.locator: Grok 4 gives kUML its narrowest Structural Fidelity win

insights.claim: The benchmark's methodological limits are stated openly: scoring is fully algorithmic rather than LLM- or human-judged, each cell is a single generation run capped at three repair attempts with no variance estimate, so the deltas are directional evidence rather than statistically established results.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Single-run benchmarks with no variance are the norm in this space — discount headline deltas accordingly when they underpin product claims.
insights.quote: Single runs carry no variance estimate, so the deltas above are directional evidence
insights.locator: The effect is real and repeats across several model families

insights.claim: TDG closes syntax gaps but not understanding gaps: in the same benchmark one model produced fully compiling C4 architecture diagrams that were semantically shallow — every construct legal, the architecture itself thin.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Compiler verification is a floor, not a quality guarantee; automated correctness checks will not substitute for domain review in agent pipelines.
insights.quote: The oracle checks well-formedness, not wisdom. TDG turns a good model into a reliable author, rather than turning a weak model into a good architect.
insights.locator: Stating the caveat plainly

insights.claim: Terraform's validate command, provider-schema distribution and language server are characterized as an entire apparatus built to recover for an external DSL what an embedded DSL's host compiler provides on day zero — with CDK for Terraform's typed provider bindings in five languages cited as the host-language move already applied to infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Frames typed IaC SDKs (Pulumi, CDK) as structurally advantaged over HCL in an agent-authored world, though the author concedes both approaches catch the same errors.
insights.quote: It is an entire apparatus with schema distribution, a dedicated validate phase, and a language server, built to recover for an external DSL what an embedded DSL's host compiler hands over on day zero.
insights.locator: Illustration Two: A Thought Experiment in Infrastructure as Code

insights.claim: The author explicitly concedes symmetry on validation currency: terraform validate checks against the provider version pinned in the lock file while a typed DSL checks against the SDK version pinned in the build file, and either pin can silently lag the live API — the embedded advantage is the same validation at near-zero incremental cost in the diagnostic format a repair loop consumes best.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: The honest framing narrows the claim to cost and diagnostic format rather than capability — useful for judging comparable vendor pitches.
insights.quote: The embedded DSL's advantage isn't more validation than Terraform's apparatus achieves; it's the same validation at near-zero incremental cost
insights.locator: Here the two approaches are symmetric, and neither wins

insights.claim: No local check of any kind reaches live cloud state — whether an AMI exists, whether permissions hold, whether quota allows — which remains invisible to both HCL and a typed DSL until something calls the real API.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Bounds how far compile-time verification can de-risk autonomous infrastructure changes — the residual risk still requires runtime guardrails.
insights.locator: What is left below both is live cloud state

insights.claim: The pattern is claimed to generalize to any domain with a typed internal DSL, a fast batch-capable compiler and a training-data-rich host language, with Gradle's Kotlin DSL, compose-style UI builders and typed configuration DSLs replacing schema-less YAML named as qualifying cases.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Predicts a migration away from schema-less YAML configuration toward typed builders — a tailwind for typed-config tooling if agent authorship keeps growing.
insights.locator: The pattern generalizes to any domain with a typed internal DSL

insights.claim: TDG's closest relative is Microsoft TypeChat, but the author distinguishes them by question: TypeChat asks whether an answer is shaped correctly against a response schema, while TDG asks whether something is a valid sentence in the domain — checking, for example, whether an association connects classifiers that actually exist.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Marks the boundary between structured-output validation (widely shipped) and semantic domain validation (largely unbuilt) — the latter is the open product space.
insights.quote: TypeChat asks "Is this answer shaped correctly?", whereas TDG asks "Is this a valid sentence in the domain?"
insights.locator: The closest relative to TDG is TypeChat

insights.claim: Grammar Prompting and the AI-oriented-grammar line both accept the premise TDG rejects — that a new syntax must exist — with the AI-oriented approach designing a more token-efficient grammar whose corpus frequency is still zero, leaving the competence gap intact and requiring teaching to bridge.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Argues that token-efficiency-optimized languages for LLMs are a dead end — relevant to any startup pitching an AI-native syntax.
insights.quote: TDG asks the questions that come before "How do you teach a foreign syntax? Why have one at all?
insights.locator: Grammar Prompting [4] and the AI-oriented-grammar line

insights.claim: TDG costs three concrete things: notational freedom (an internal DSL reads more slowly than a purpose-built compact notation), sunk investment in working external DSLs, and a host-language commitment that is a real first-time cost for domain-expert audiences who have never seen a lambda.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: The domain-expert onboarding cost is the practical blocker in regulated and engineering verticals where non-programmers author models.
insights.locator: What This Costs You

insights.claim: The author frames a second design dimension now standing beside classic DSL readability: how close the language sits to what its most probable future author already knows and how much verification the toolchain supplies for free — with weight shifting toward this second question as DSLs are increasingly generated and read by models rather than humans.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: If model authorship share keeps rising, this reweighting propagates to API, schema and config design across the whole developer-tools market.
insights.quote: How close does the language already sit to what its most probable future author can already do
insights.locator: The Second Question

insights.claim: The author stresses nothing here depends on future research — the host languages, compilers and teaching-channel protocol all exist today — and explicitly scopes the recommendation to new DSLs rather than migrating working ones.
insights.speaker: Irakli Betchvaia
insights.so_what: Implementable-now framing with a deliberately narrow migration ask, which makes adoption plausible but slow — expect impact at greenfield projects first.
insights.quote: Nothing here waits on future research.
insights.locator: The Second Question
